items.prompt: Describe these fictional education routes and give a reasoned judgement for a learner seeking recognised technical skills. Here, a community apprenticeship illustrates traditional education through local craft learning and daily participation; it provides no formal qualification. A reachable college course illustrates modern institutional education through technical theory and an assessed qualification, but charges affordable fees and reduces earning time. Both are feasible.
items.canonical_answer: Traditional community learning offers locally relevant practice without course fees, but in this case gives no formal qualification and may cover a narrower range of technical knowledge. Modern college education provides structured theory and an assessed qualification, but involves fees and less time for earning. College better fits the stated aim of recognised technical skills if its qualification is accepted and costs remain manageable. Community learning may better fit a different aim centred on local craft practice. Judge the stated routes rather than assume that all traditional or modern education has identical quality.
marking_guidance: Description: identify the traditional/community and modern/institutional routes and their stated features.
Judgement: weigh practical relevance and recognition against fees and time for earning, using the learner’s stated aim.
Reason: develop a conditional conclusion; do not invent an allowance or recognised apprenticeship assessment.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain which fictional ICT programme better fits accessible learning. A equips more schools with shared devices, basic teacher training and power. B equips fewer schools with more teaching support, accessible materials and reliable connectivity. Both operate, and the same budget covers one.
items.canonical_answer: A spreads a usable minimum of equipment and training more widely, but shared access may limit learning time. B offers richer teaching support and access arrangements, potentially helping learners with more varied needs, but covers fewer schools. Prefer B where unsupported learning needs are the main barrier, or A where basic access across many schools is the urgent priority. Monitor actual use and learning rather than device totals, and plan how the other group will later be reached.
marking_guidance: Judgement: compare genuine benefits and costs against the stated aim.
Reason: develop each option using supplied evidence, weigh the trade-off, and give a conditional conclusion.

items.prompt: State (a) the distinction between formal and non-formal education [2]. Explain (b) why a fictional evening skills programme with tools can be more usable to working adults than daytime-only provision, even if both have equal admission rules [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) Within the recognised structured system versus organised learning outside its main system. (b) Working adults may be unable to attend daytime lessons because attendance conflicts with their paid work. Evening provision removes that stated time conflict, though its actual travel and safety arrangements still need checking. Available tools allow learners to practise the skills rather than receive theory alone. Equal admission rules do not supply either usable time or practical equipment, so judge effective access and learning opportunities from these delivery conditions as well as formal eligibility.
marking_guidance: Point: organisational distinction [2].
Development: use both timing and tools to explain access and skill development [4].
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.
